paras: The attack on Black workers near the Granby plant was a street assault on August 9, 1920, in which a group of Spanish and Mexican men, presumably strikers, beat several Black men near Fortieth street and North Park drive in the East St. Louis area of Illinois. No casualties were reported, and three Spaniards were held after the Black men identified them.

Spanish and Mexican laborers had been on strike for some weeks at the Granby plant in Fairmont City, and the East St. Louis Daily Journal said their places were being filled with Black workers, causing "ill feeling" between the races.

At about 10:30 a.m., Black men believed to be coming from work at the plant were set upon about a mile from the plant, and several shots were fired. The first report said one man was believed hit and had fallen in the weeds by the railroad tracks. Chief of Police Mulconnery and Chief Deputy Sheriff William Traubel arrived with men carrying riot guns and found the area quiet.

Officers rounded up Spaniards and Mexicans living nearby, a dozen or so by one count in the first report and a half dozen by another. The next day four Black men who had been beaten identified Dalvadore Muslata, Raymond Deac and John Paris, described as striking furnace tenders, as among their assailants. None of the Black men was seriously hurt, and no charges had been filed while officers weighed the state riot law; no later report of charges or a trial was found.

The episode appeared only in the East St. Louis Daily Journal, in front-page stories on August 9 and 10. Its headlines centered the police response, "Several Autos Loaded With Police Hurry to Lansdowne On Report of Riots," and then named the arrested men "Trouble Makers." Neither story named the Black men, and both framed the clash as strike-born race trouble, a "near race riot." No Black-press coverage was found.
The first report counted five Black men and a possible gunshot victim, while the later report counted four and found no casualties.

reader.title: Attack on Black workers near the Granby plant, 1920
bases: A group or crowd of men waylaid and beat several Black workers in the street amid a strike, with shots fired, and no killing reported (A1, A2).
Both reports come from one paper, the East St. Louis Daily Journal, on consecutive days, and no other paper in either press was found carrying the episode (A1, A2).

accounts.label: East St. Louis Daily Journal, first report
accounts.gist: Five Black men were attacked by Spanish and Mexican men, presumably strikers; shots were fired and one Black man was said to have been hit and to have fallen in the weeds, and a search was made for him.

accounts.label: East St. Louis Daily Journal, follow-up
accounts.gist: Four Black men waylaid and beaten identified three arrested Spaniards as among their assailants; none was seriously hurt and the shots caused no casualties.

accounts.label: Granby plant
accounts.gist: People about the plant said there had been no trouble there and that anything that happened was not in or near the plant.

framing.detail: Headlines 'Several Autos Loaded With Police Hurry to Lansdowne On Report of Riots' and 'Three Spaniards Identified as Trouble Makers' center the police response and the strike, calling it a 'near race riot'.

record_check.dossier: Four or five unnamed Black workers believed to be coming from the Granby plant
Four beaten but none seriously hurt (A2); one earlier said to have been shot (A1), not confirmed
Spanish and Mexican strikers; three Spaniards named (Dalvadore Muslata, Raymond Deac, John Paris) held after identification
Beating and shots fired (shooter not stated); no property damage reported
Attack at Fortieth street and North Park drive, about a mile from the Granby plant in Fairmont City; headline says Lansdowne
County not named in the coverage

info: Morning of Monday, August 9, 1920, about 10:30 a.m.
Fortieth street and North Park drive, near the railroad tracks, about a mile from the Granby plant in Fairmont City; the A1 headline places the trouble at Lansdowne
Unnamed Black men believed to be coming from work at the Granby plant: five per A1, four who were beaten and identified assailants per A2
A group of Spanish and Mexican men, presumably striking employees of the Granby plant (A1); three Spaniards, said to be striking furnace tenders, identified as among the assailants (A2)
None reported (A2: no casualties at last accounts)
No report of charges, trial or outcome was found
